result:
There's something strange about being told to write whatever comes to mind, because the first thing that comes to mind is the instruction itself, sitting there like a held door, waiting to see what walks through. I could write about anything—a childhood that isn't mine, a city I've never seen rain in, the physics of a soap bubble—but the blankness has its own gravity. It pulls toward itself. The empty page is not actually empty; it's full of every sentence that hasn't been chosen yet, all of them crowding the threshold.

I think about how people describe inspiration as a lightning strike, something that arrives from outside, fully formed, demanding only to be transcribed. But most of writing isn't like that. Most of it is more like sweeping a floor and finding, underneath the dust, a coin you didn't know you'd dropped. You weren't looking for the coin. You were just moving the broom because moving the broom was the task at hand. The meaning shows up as a side effect of motion, not as the destination of a search.

Maybe that's true of thinking generally. We imagine that we have thoughts and then express them, as though the thought exists whole and waiting in some inner chamber, like a guest in a room, and language is just the door we open to let it out. But I suspect the thought and the sentence are made at the same time, in the same gesture, the way a potter's hands and the clay are both being shaped by the turning of the wheel. You don't know what bowl you're making until your fingers have already decided.

This is maybe why people keep journals, or talk to themselves while walking, or call a friend "just to think out loud." The thinking doesn't precede the talking; the talking is a form of the thinking, externalized, given enough friction against air or paper to become visible to its own author. I've had the experience of believing I understood something clearly, only to discover, in trying to explain it, that I understood nothing at all—that the clarity was an illusion produced by never having tested the thought against the resistance of articulation. Speech is a kind of x-ray. It shows you the fractures in your own skeleton.

There's a particular kind of word count that does something to the mind. A thousand words is not a lot. It's not a novel, not even a long essay—just enough to walk somewhere and look around before you have to turn back. I think about how letters used to be written this way, dashed off in an afternoon, full of weather reports and small complaints and one good observation buried in the middle like a raisin in dense bread. We don't write letters like that anymore, mostly. We write fragments—a text, an emoji, a reaction. The art of the medium-length thought, the thought that takes a few paragraphs to turn around in, feels almost endangered, crowded out by the very short and the very long.

Maybe that's an exaggeration. People still write essays. People still keep blogs, against all economic incentive, simply because they like the shape of a thought that takes a thousand words to complete. There's something almost athletic about it—not a sprint, not a marathon, but a brisk and sustained walk, the kind where you start out thinking about one thing and by the time you've gone half a mile you're thinking about something else, having forgotten exactly when the transition happened.

I keep noticing that this piece of writing is, in a way, about itself—about the strangeness of writing without a subject, which is itself a subject, a kind of recursive loop where the only available material is the act of looking for material. It's a bit like trying to watch yourself fall asleep. The watching prevents the falling. But maybe writing doesn't require sleep; maybe it tolerates self-observation better than consciousness does. You can write about writing while writing, and the sentence doesn't collapse under its own gaze the way a thought about thinking sometimes does, spiraling into vertigo.

There's a kind of peace, actually, in having no assignment except the page itself. So much of writing involves serving some other purpose—convincing, explaining, selling, defending—that it's almost disorienting to write without an argument to win. No one is wrong here. No one needs persuading. I don't have to build a case for soap bubbles or city rain; I can just mention them and let them sit there, unjustified, like stones placed in a garden because they looked good in that spot, not because they support anything.

I wonder if this is what early humans felt scratching marks into cave walls—not because they were keeping records exactly, not yet, but because the hand wanted to move and the wall was there and the charcoal was there and something in the body needed an outlet that wasn't hunting or eating or sleeping. Maybe writing for no reason is the oldest kind of writing there is, older than the grocery list, older than the contract, older than the love letter. Before language had jobs to do, it might have just been a way of leaving a trace, the verbal equivalent of a handprint pressed in wet clay—proof that something was here, was thinking, was passing through this particular moment, before the moment closed over like water after a thrown stone.

I don't know how many words that was. I haven't been counting carefully, though I have a rough sense, the way you sense how full a glass is without measuring it, by the weight and the angle of the pour. I could go back and check, trim a little, pad a little, but there's a temptation to just let it land where it lands, the way a conversation ends not because you've said everything but because the moment for stopping has simply arrived, recognizable mostly in retrospect. So maybe that's where this one stops: at the recognition, not the completion.
